entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 9 Eze 9:1-11 . Continuation of the Preceding Vision: The Sealing of the Faithful. 1. cried-- contrasted with their "cry" for mercy ( Eze 8:18 ) is the "cry" here for vengeance, showing how vain was the former. them that have charge-- literally, officers; so "officers" ( Is 60:17 ), having the city in charge, not to guard, but to punish it. The angels who as "watchers" fulfil God's judgments ( Da 4:13 , 17, 23; 10:20 , 21 ); the "princes" ( Jr 39:3 ) of Nebuchadnezzar's army were under their guidance. draw near-- in the Hebrew intensive, "to draw near quickly."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11086"/><div sID="gen19973" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11086"/><hi type="bold">2. clothed with linen--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">7</reference>). His clothing marked his office as distinct from that of the six officers of vengeance; "linen" characterized the high priest (<reference osisRef="Lev.16.4">Le 16:4</reference>); emblematic of purity. The same garment is assigned to the angel of the Lord (for whom Michael is but another name) by the contemporary prophet Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">Da 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.6">12:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">7</reference>). Therefore the intercessory High Priest in heaven must be meant (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.12">Zec 1:12</reference>). The six with Him are His subordinates; therefore He is said to be "among them," literally, "in the midst of them," as their recognized Lord (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>). He appears as a "man," implying His incarnation; as "one" (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>). Salvation is peculiarly assigned to Him, and so He bears the "inkhorn" in order to "mark" His elect (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.7">Ex 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.9.4">9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">13:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">20:4</reference>), and to write their names in His book of life (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.8">Re 13:8</reference>). As Oriental scribes suspend their inkhorn at their side in the present day, and as a "scribe of the host is found in Assyrian inscriptions accompanying the host" to number the heads of the slain, so He stands ready for the work before Him. "The higher gate" was probably where now the gate of Damascus is. The six with Him make up the sacred and perfect number, seven (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zec 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>). The executors of judgment on the wicked, in Scripture teaching, are good, not bad, angels; the bad have permitted to them the trial of the pious (<reference osisRef="Job.1.12">Job 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>). The judgment is executed by Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.22">Joh 5:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>) through the six (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">25:31</reference>); so beautifully does the Old Testament harmonize with the New Testament. The seven come "from the way of the north"; for it was there the idolatries were seen, and from the same quarter must proceed the judgment (Babylon lying northeast of Judea). So <reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Mt 24:28</reference>.<div eID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood--</hi>the attitude of waiting reverently for Jehovah's commands.<div eID="gen19974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brazen altar--</hi>the altar of burnt offerings, not the altar of incense, which was of gold. They "stood" there to imply reverent obedience; for there God gave His answers to prayer [Calvin]; also as being about to slay victims to God's justice, they stand where sacrifices are usually slain [Grotius], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.39.17">Eze 39:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.6">Is 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">Jr 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.10">46:10</reference>). <div eID="gen19975" type="x-p"/>

The same garment is assigned to the angel of the Lord (for whom Michael is but another name) by the contemporary prophet Daniel ( Da 10:5 ; 12:6 , 7 ). Therefore the intercessory High Priest in heaven must be meant ( Zec 1:12 ). The six with Him are His subordinates; therefore He is said to be "among them," literally, "in the midst of them," as their recognized Lord ( He 1:6 ). He appears as a "man," implying His incarnation; as "one" (compare 1Ti 2:5 ). Salvation is peculiarly assigned to Him, and so He bears the "inkhorn" in order to "mark" His elect ( Eze 9:4 ; compare Ex 12:7 ; Re 7:3 ; 9:4 ; 13:16 , 17 ; 20:4 ), and to write their names in His book of life ( Re 13:8 ). As Oriental scribes suspend their inkhorn at their side in the present day, and as a "scribe of the host is found in Assyrian inscriptions accompanying the host" to number the heads of the slain, so He stands ready for the work before Him. "The higher gate" was probably where now the gate of Damascus is. The six with Him make up the sacred and perfect number, seven ( Zec 3:9 ; Re 5:6 ). The judgment is executed by Him ( Eze 10:2 , 7 ; Joh 5:22 , 27 ) through the six ( Mt 13:41 ; 25:31 ); so beautifully does the Old Testament harmonize with the New Testament. God--</hi>which had heretofore, as a bright cloud, rested on the mercy seat between the cherubim in the holy of holies (<reference osisRef="2Sam.6.2">2Sa 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>); its departure was the presage of the temple being given up to ruin; its going from the inner sanctuary to the threshold without, towards the officers standing at the altar outside, was in order to give them the commission of vengeance. <div eID="gen19976" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11088"/><div sID="gen19977" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11088"/><hi type="bold">4. midst of ... city ... midst of Jerusalem--</hi>This twofold designation marks more emphatically the scene of the divine judgments.<div eID="gen19977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a mark--</hi>literally, the Hebrew letter Tau, the last in the alphabet, used as a mark ("my sign," <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>, Margin); literally, Tau; originally written in the form of a cross, which Tertullian explains as referring to the badge and only means of salvation, the cross of Christ. But nowhere in Scripture are the words which are now employed as names of letters used to denote the letters themselves or their figures [Vitringa]. The noun here is cognate to the verb, "mark a mark." So in <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference> no particular mark is specified. We seal what we wish to guard securely. When all things else on earth are confounded, God will secure His people from the common ruin. God gives the first charge as to their safety before He orders the punishment of the rest (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">21</reference>). So in the case of Lot and Sodom (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.22">Ge 19:22</reference>); also the Egyptian first-born were not slain till Israel had time to sprinkle the blood-mark, ensuring their safety (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3">Re 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.9">Am 9:9</reference>). So the early Christians had Pella provided as a refuge for them, before the destruction of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the foreheads--</hi>the most conspicuous part of the person, to imply how their safety would be manifested to all (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.15.11">Jr 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11-Jer.39.18">39:11-18</reference>). It was customary thus to mark worshippers (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">Re 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.1">14:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.9">9</reference>) and servants. So the Church of England marks the forehead with the sign of the cross in baptizing. At the exodus the mark was on the houses, for then it was families; here, it is on the foreheads, for it is individuals whose safety is guaranteed.<div eID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sigh and ... cry--</hi>similarly sounding verbs in Hebrew, as in English Version, expressing the prolonged sound of their grief. "Sigh" implies their inward grief ("groanings which cannot be uttered," <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>); "cry," the outward expression of it. So Lot (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.7">2Pe 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). Tenderness should characterize the man of God, not harsh sternness in opposing the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.53">Psa 119:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.136">136</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">2Co 12:21</reference>); at the same time zeal for the honor of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen19980" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11090"/><div sID="gen19982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11090"/><hi type="bold">6. come not near any ... upon whom ... mark--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.9.4">Re 9:4</reference>). It may be objected that Daniel, Jeremiah, and others were carried away, whereas many of the vilest were left in the land. But God does not promise believers exemption from all suffering, but only from what will prove really and lastingly hurtful to them. His sparing the ungodly turns to their destruction and leaves them without excuse [Calvin]. However, the prophecy waits a fuller and final fulfilment, for <reference osisRef="Rev.7.3-Rev.7.8">Re 7:3-8</reference>, in ages long after Babylon, foretells, as still future, the same sealing of a remnant (one hundred forty-four thousand) of Israel previous to the final outpouring of wrath on the rest of the nation; the correspondence is exact; the same pouring of fire from the altar follows the marking of the remnant in both (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.8.5">Re 8:5</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.2">Eze 10:2</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">Zec 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">14:2</reference>, distinguish the remnant from the rest of Israel.<div eID="gen19982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">begin at ... sanctuary--</hi>For in it the greatest abominations had been committed; it had lost the reality of consecration by the blood of victims sacrificed to idols; it must, therefore, lose its semblance by the dead bodies of the slain idolaters (<reference osisRef="Ezek.9.7">Eze 9:7</reference>). God's heaviest wrath falls on those who have sinned against the highest privileges; these are made to feel it first (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.18">18</reference>). He hates sin most in those nearest to Him; for example, the priests, &c.<div eID="gen19983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ancient men--</hi>the seventy elders. <div eID="gen19984" type="x-p"/>
